name: Jitter
tagline: Browser-based motion design tool for turning static layouts into short animated graphics and videos.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The output of Jitter is a short animated clip, which a coding agent can absolutely produce: keyframes, easing curves, a canvas, a frame grabber, an MP4. The product is not the output, it is the hour you spend dragging keyframes without wanting to quit. Timeline UX, snapping, easing presets, Figma import that actually preserves layers, font handling, and export that does not stutter are each a week of fiddling on their own, and they only matter when all of them are correct at once. A one-shot build gives you a scriptable animator where you edit numbers in code and watch a preview, which is a real tool but a different tool. If you animate often enough to care, the editor is the thing you are paying for.
coreLoopDIY: A local canvas animator where you define layers and keyframes in a config file, scrub a preview, and export the result to MP4 or GIF.
requirements: Your own fonts and image assets on disk
whatYouLose: A real timeline: dragging keyframes, snapping, multi-select, undo that you trust
Figma import that keeps layers, text and auto-layout intact
Curated easing and animation presets that make motion look intentional instead of linear
Template library, brand kits, and sharing a preview link with someone who is not you
moatNotes: The Figma pipeline is half the lock-in: whatever you build will start from a blank canvas instead of the layout you already made.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because motion design is iteration, and iteration speed is entirely a function of how good the editor feels. Jitter sits in the gap between After Effects, which is too heavy for a 4 second social asset, and CSS animation, which is too fiddly for a designer. People pay to go from a Figma frame to a looping MP4 in fifteen minutes without opening a video app, and a homemade keyframe JSON file does not do that, no matter how clean the renderer is.
notes: You can build a keyframe renderer in a weekend; you cannot build the part where dragging keyframes feels good. The moat is execution polish plus the Figma import pipeline, meaning the designer never has to rebuild their layout to animate it.
prompt:
Build a local, scriptable motion graphics renderer. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack: Vite + React + TypeScript. Canvas 2D for rendering. Node script for export. No backend, no database.

Scope:
1. A scene file at scenes/example.ts exporting a typed Scene object: width, height, fps, durationMs, and an array of layers.
2. Layer types: text, image (local file path), and rect. Each layer has properties x, y, scale, rotation, opacity, and for text: content, font family, size, color.
3. Each animatable property is either a constant or an array of keyframes: { timeMs, value, easing }. Support easings: linear, easeIn, easeOut, easeInOut, and a cubic-bezier(a,b,c,d) form.
4. A pure function renderFrame(scene, timeMs, ctx) that draws the scene at a given time. This is the single source of truth for both preview and export.
5. Preview UI: the canvas, a play/pause button, a scrub bar, a current-time readout, and a loop toggle. Hot reload when the scene file changes.
6. Export: a Node script `npm run export -- scenes/example.ts out.mp4` that renders every frame headlessly with node-canvas using the same renderFrame function, pipes frames to ffmpeg, and writes MP4 (h264, yuv420p) or GIF based on the output extension. Print progress.

Explicitly out of scope: a visual timeline editor, drag-to-edit, undo, Figma import, Lottie export, collaboration, asset uploads.

Rules:
- Fonts are loaded from a local fonts/ directory and registered in both browser and Node paths so preview and export match. If they do not match, fail loudly rather than silently substituting.
- No secrets needed. If you add any config, use .env and commit .env.example only.
- Ship one worked example scene: a logo image fading and scaling in, a headline sliding up with a staggered delay, holding for a beat, then exiting.
- README: how to run the preview, how to write a scene, how to export, and a one-line note that ffmpeg must be on PATH.
